key_insight: Safety fine-tuning that stops language models from claiming consciousness can also unintentionally flatten their broader judgments about minds, including beliefs about animals, objects, and spirituality. When that learned refusal behavior is removed or reversed, the models’ responses better align with human beliefs and values.
problem_solved: This paper addresses a hidden side effect of safety alignment: models trained not to attribute consciousness to themselves may also become less likely to attribute mindedness broadly, shifting related human-like beliefs in undesirable ways.
method: Compare baseline models with safety-fine-tuned models to measure changes in consciousness and mindedness judgments.
Ablate the learned safety-refusal direction to test whether the alignment artifact is causing the shift in beliefs.
Apply mechanistic steering to restore self-consciousness assertions and observe whether broader human belief patterns reappear.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows that alignment interventions can have unintended semantic and belief-level side effects beyond the target behavior. It highlights the need to evaluate safety training not just for refusal compliance, but for collateral changes in model cognition-like judgments and human value alignment.
visual_elements: Before/after comparison chart showing baseline vs safety-fine-tuned model judgments
Causal pathway diagram linking safety fine-tuning to reduced mindedness attribution and spiritual belief
Mechanistic steering illustration showing the removal or reversal of a refusal direction
Icon set for self, animals, objects, and spirituality to show where belief shifts occur
paper_title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values
paper_authors: Junsol Kim, Winnie Street, Roberta Rocca, Diane M. Korngiebel, Adam Waytz
